lines.text: He who had the first choice came forward and in a moment chose the greatest tyranny. His mind had been darkened by folly, and he had not thought out the whole matter before he chose. When he saw what was in the lot, he began to beat his breast, and blamed chance and the gods and everything rather than himself. He had lived in a well-ordered city in his former life, but his virtue was a matter of habit only, and he had no philosophy.
lines.say: He who had the first choice came forward and in a moment chose the greatest tyranny. His mind had been darkened by folly, and he had not thought out the whole matter before he chose. When he saw what was in the lot, he began to beat his breast, and blamed chance and the gods and everything rather than himself. He had lived in a well-ordered city in his former life, but his virtue was a matter of habit only, and he had no philosophy.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Last of all, a weathered traveller searches through the lives left lying on the ground, and smiles at a plain one.
lines.say: Last of all, a weathered traveller searches through the lives left lying on the ground, and smiles at a plain one.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: There came also the soul of Odysseus, and his lot was the last of them all. The recollection of former toils had disenchanted him of ambition, and he went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares. He found it lying about, neglected by everybody else, and said that he would have done the same had his lot been first, and that he was delighted to have it.
lines.say: There came also the soul of Odysseus, and his lot was the last of them all. The recollection of former toils had disenchanted him of ambition, and he went about for a considerable time in search of the life of a private man who had no cares. He found it lying about, neglected by everybody else, and said that he would have done the same had his lot been first, and that he was delighted to have it.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: Then the souls drank from the river of Unmindfulness, and each one as he drank forgot all things. Er alone was hindered from drinking. And in the morning, awaking suddenly, he found himself lying on the pyre.
lines.say: Then the souls drank from the river of Unmindfulness, and each one as he drank forgot all things. Air alone was hindered from drinking. And in the morning, awaking suddenly, he found himself lying on the pyre.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The sky above the courtyard is turning grey.
lines.say: The sky above the courtyard is turning grey.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: And thus, Glaucon, the tale has been saved and has not perished, and will save us if we are obedient to the word spoken. Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods. And it shall be well with us, both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.
lines.say: And thus, Glaucon, the tale has been saved and has not perished, and will save us if we are obedient to the word spoken. Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods. And it shall be well with us, both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: A long silence. Adeimantus has fallen asleep. Glaucon's eyes close, his head drops against his brother's shoulder.
lines.say: A long silence. Adee-mantus has fallen asleep. Glaucon's eyes close, his head drops against his brother's shoulder.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Socrates rises, steps carefully between the sleepers, and crosses the courtyard to Julian.
lines.say: Socrates rises, steps carefully between the sleepers, and crosses the courtyard to Julian.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: You came down to the Piraeus to see how they would celebrate the festival, which was a new thing.
lines.say: You came down to the Pie-reeus to see how they would celebrate the festival, which was a new thing.

lines.speaker: Julian
lines.text: You knew I was here. The whole night.
lines.say: You knew I was here. The whole night.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: A man who casts no shadow is easy to find, in a room full of shadows.
lines.say: A man who casts no shadow is easy to find, in a room full of shadows.

lines.speaker: Julian
lines.text: Glaucon was right about the ring. I could have taken anything in this house. Walked into the Assembly. Read every letter in Athens.
lines.say: Glaucon was right about the ring. I could have taken anything in this house. Walked into the Assembly. Read every letter in Athens.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: And what did you take?
lines.say: And what did you take?

lines.speaker: Julian
lines.text: Nothing. I listened.
lines.say: Nothing. I listened.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: Then you have answered Glaucon better than I did all night, and in fewer words.
lines.say: Then you have answered Glaucon better than I did all night, and in fewer words.

lines.speaker: Julian
lines.text: Socrates, I know how your story ends. The cave. The ones who try to lead the others up.
lines.say: Socrates, I know how your story ends. The cave. The ones who try to lead the others up.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: Then keep it to yourself. A man should not be told the end of his play while he is still acting in it.
lines.say: Then keep it to yourself. A man should not be told the end of his play while he is still acting in it.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: In your lounge, you showed me your cave. Tonight I have shown you mine. It is the same den, Julian. Yours has better lamps.
lines.say: In your lounge, you showed me your cave. Tonight I have shown you mine. It is the same den, Julian. Yours has better lamps.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: He folds Julian's fingers over the ring, bezel outward.
lines.say: He folds Julian's fingers over the ring, bezel outward.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: Go down. Your city has need of a man who has seen the sun and come back with his eyes. And keep it turned this way. Let them see you.
lines.say: Go down. Your city has need of a man who has seen the sun and come back with his eyes. And keep it turned this way. Let them see you.

lines.speaker: Julian
lines.text: Maintain the mirror.
lines.say: Maintain the mirror.

lines.speaker: Socrates
lines.text: Guard the water.
lines.say: Guard the water.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Julian turns the ring a full circle. The smell of salt and thyme gives way to smog and botanical vapor. The air shimmers, and he is gone.
lines.say: Julian turns the ring a full circle. The smell of salt and thyme gives way to smog and botanical vapor. The air shimmers, and he is gone.
